items.abstract: <jats:p>Research at the interface of biodiversity conservation, urban forestry, and urban green space spans ecology, forestry, landscape planning, environmental management, and public health, making its intellectual structure difficult to apprehend through narrative review alone. This study maps a corpus of 3747 documents published from 2006 to 17 August 2026, retrieved from the OpenAlex API on 13 October 2026 after integrity checking and deduplication. Performance analysis, country-level collaboration networks, lexical co-occurrence on titles and abstracts (abstract coverage 82.6% after supplementation), strategic mapping, thematic evolution, co-citation, and bibliographic coupling were computed with scripts released with the article; stochastic community partitions were evaluated over 200 seeded runs. Across the complete years 2006–2025, retrieved annual output increased at a compound annual rate of 15.89%. The corpus spans 1316 journals and affiliations in 124 countries. China leads publication output, whereas Germany and the USA occupy the strongest brokerage positions in the collaboration network. Author-derived text resolves six lexical clusters (modularity = 0.442), in which health and planning vocabulary joins climate and green-infrastructure terms and carbon vocabulary joins tree and plant species, and co-citation of the 200 most cited references identifies six communities (modularity = 0.507). More than half of the corpus (54.9%) enters only through green-space terms, and removing these documents changes the lexical partition substantially; a replica of a prior green-space mapping shows that urban-forestry terms distinguish the corpus. The mapped literature is increasingly connected to climate, health, and planning agendas.</jats:p>
title: Mapping Biodiversity Research on Urban Forests and Green Spaces: Conceptual and Intellectual Structures and Country-Level Collaboration

items.abstract: <jats:p>The long-eared hedgehog, Hemiechinus auritus, has the broadest distribution among Erinaceidae, yet its intraspecific taxonomy remains contentious, with three to six subspecies recognized. We examined the phylogeographic structure of the species across nearly its entire distribution range using two mitochondrial genes (cytb, COI) for 153 specimens from 103 localities, complemented by complete mitogenomes for seven individuals. Phylogenetic reconstructions recovered five deeply divergent, well-supported mitochondrial lineages (p-distances 2–4%): Northern, Eastern, Transcaucasian, South-western and Southern. The Southern lineage, which includes specimens from the type locality of H. a. megalotis, was recovered as the basal branch, whereas the Northern and Eastern lineages formed a derived clade. Demographic analyses indicated recent postglacial expansion in the Northern and Eastern lineages, but not in the Southern and South-western lineages. Species distribution modelling reconstructed Pleistocene range fragmentation during glacial maxima, with divergence among lineages dated to the late Middle and Late Pleistocene. The mitochondrial lineages are partly congruent with the main morphological subspecies, although the status of H. a. megalotis and H. collaris requires further scrutiny. Our results indicate that H. auritus may represent a complex of several divergent lineages, whose evolutionary independence and taxonomic status should be tested with nuclear genomic data.</jats:p>
title: The Most Successful Species Among Spiny Hedgehogs: Mitochondrial Phylogeography of Hemiechinus auritus (Gmelin, 1770) (Erinaceidae, Mammalia)

items.abstract: <jats:p>The truffle genus Genea plays an important role as an ectomycorrhizal fungus, yet its taxonomy, evolutionary relationships, and ecological behaviour remain poorly understood globally. This study describes Genea budensis sp. nov. and reports G. arenaria and G. zamorana for the first time from Hungary, based on morphological examination and phylogenetic analyses of ITS and LSU sequences. The new species Genea budensis sp. nov., found in the Buda Mountains in Hungary, is characterized by a warty, scale-covered surface peridium; spores ornamented with dense, cone-shaped projections, with some of them being blunt-tipped or bud-like in form. This discovery also marks the first documented occurrence of both Genea zamorana and G. arenaria within Hungary. These findings expand the documented diversity and geographic distribution of Genea in Hungary and provide additional morphological and molecular data for future taxonomic studies of the genus.</jats:p>
title: Expanding the Known Diversity of the Truffle Genus Genea: One New Species and Two New Records from Hungary

items.abstract: <jats:p>Fritillaria mardinensis Balos, C. Çeçen, Köse & Sonay sp. nov. (Liliaceae) is described as a new species from Mardin Province, southeastern Türkiye. It is morphologically similar to F. armena and F. zagrica but differs from the related species F. armena and F. zagrica by its longer stem structure, yellowish hairy/striped mosaic pattern at the tepal tips, linear nectary structure, and capsule morphology containing longitudinally dark green striped, winged seeds. Diagnostic characters, description, detailed illustration, geographical distribution, conservation assessment, observations and taxonomic comments regarding the new species are given. ITS sequence data are compatible with the placement of the species in Fritillaria but are uninformative at the species level, as F. mardinensis falls in an unresolved polytomy with F. armena and other congeners; its delimitation therefore rests on morphology.</jats:p>
title: Fritillaria mardinensis (Liliaceae), a New Species from Southeastern Türkiye

items.abstract: <jats:p>Conspicuous tropical fishes are readily detected by sea users, but repeated sightings and uncertain identifications can distort occurrence histories. We reviewed source-traceable Mediterranean records of Paracanthurus hepatus and Heniochus intermedius through 1 October 2026 and documented two additional video observations: P. hepatus at Cap Dramont, France, on 10 September 2024, and Heniochus cf. intermedius near Sorrento, Italy, on 23 June 2026. Five P. hepatus observation episodes represent at least four individuals. The French observation was approximately 79 m from the site of a fish removed in July and 0.92 km from another individual last observed five days earlier; it may represent the latter fish after displacement or an additional individual. The reconciled Heniochus chronology contains 27 reported occurrence entries across 11 countries: 14 retained as H. intermedius and 13 as H. cf. intermedius. Aquarium release is the leading hypothesis for P. hepatus, whereas Suez Canal dispersal is plausible for H. intermedius; individual pathways remain unverified. Source reconciliation and conservative identification improve citizen-science contributions to Mediterranean biodiversity monitoring.</jats:p>
title: Mediterranean Records of the Alien Fishes Paracanthurus hepatus and Heniochus intermedius: Source Reconciliation and New Observations from France and Italy

items.abstract: <jats:p>Cliff habitats support distinctive plant communities, yet the vegetation characteristics associated with the natural occurrence of Dendrobium moniliforme remain poorly understood. This study characterized plant communities associated with the occurrence of D. moniliforme on a coastal cliff of Seonyudo Island, Republic of Korea, using unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based vegetation surveys. A total of 56 plots, comprising 13 occurrence and 43 absence plots, were surveyed, and plant diversity, taxonomic composition, and life-form composition were compared between the two groups. Species richness was significantly lower in occurrence plots, whereas Shannon diversity was significantly higher. Plant community composition differed significantly between occurrence and absence plots (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.075, p = 0.0005), with several species contributing to the observed compositional differences. Life-form composition also differed significantly between the two groups (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.045, p = 0.028), with occurrence plots tending to show greater relative cover of chamaephytes, hemicryptophytes, geophytes, and epiphytes. These findings suggest that, within the studied coastal cliff, the occurrence of D. moniliforme is associated with differences in surrounding vegetation composition rather than simply greater species richness, providing site-specific baseline information for habitat characterization and conservation.</jats:p>
title: Plant Community Characteristics Associated with the Occurrence of the Endangered Epiphytic Orchid Dendrobium moniliforme on a Coastal Cliff in Korea
